Front:
UV disinfection primarily inactivates microorganisms by:
a. Damaging nucleic acids (DNA/RNA)
b. Removing cell walls
c. Oxidizing metals
d. Stripping gases
Back: Answer: a. Damaging nucleic acids (DNA/RNA)

Front:
UV dose is the product of:
a. UV intensity and exposure time
b. Lamp power and lamp age
c. Color and turbidity
d. Flow and temperature
Back: Answer: a. UV intensity and exposure time

Front:
UV transmittance (UVT) is a measure of:
a. How much UV light passes through the water
b. Chlorine residual
c. pH
d. Turbidity only
Back: Answer: a. How much UV light passes through the water

Front:
Low UVT water requires:
a. Higher lamp power or more reactors to achieve the same dose
b. Less lamp power
c. No UV treatment
d. Only chlorine treatment
Back: Answer: a. Higher lamp power or more reactors to achieve the same dose

Front:
UV/AOP (advanced oxidation) combines UV with:
radicals
a. A chemical such as hydrogen peroxide or ozone to form hydroxyl
b. Lime softening
c. Ion exchange resin
d. Sand filtration
Back: Answer: a. A chemical such as hydrogen peroxide or ozone to form hydroxyl

Front:
AOP is particularly effective at:
a. Oxidizing trace organic compounds and some taste/odor compounds
b. Removing hardness only
c. Removing dissolved gases only
d. Removing suspended solids only
Back: Answer: a. Oxidizing trace organic compounds and some taste/odor compounds

Front:
Excess peroxide downstream of UV/AOP can:
a. Increase residual oxidant that may need quenching
b. Increase turbidity
c. Reduce UV dose
d. Increase scaling
Back: Answer: a. Increase residual oxidant that may need quenching

Front:
UV reactors typically require:
a. Clean quartz sleeves to maintain adequate intensity
b. Excess chlorine residual
c. High turbidity
d. High hardness
Back: Answer: a. Clean quartz sleeves to maintain adequate intensity

Front:
Online UV intensity sensors must be:
a. Calibrated and kept clean for accurate dose control
b. Left untouched once installed
c. Operated only in manual mode
d. Used only for alarm, not control
Back: Answer: a. Calibrated and kept clean for accurate dose control

Front:
A sudden drop in UV dose with normal UVT and lamp status often
indicates:
a. Fouled intensity sensors or incorrect readings
b. Low pH
c. High hardness
d. High alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. Fouled intensity sensors or incorrect readings

Front:
Disinfection by chloramines is often used to:
potential

c. Increase CT significantly

Front:

c. Add more ammonia
d. Remove all storage tanks from service

Front:
pH adjustment after RO is often required to:
a. Reduce corrosivity and adjust finished water alkalinity
b. Increase turbidity
c. Increase TDS
d. Eliminate the need for disinfectant
Back: Answer: a. Reduce corrosivity and adjust finished water alkalinity

Front:
Caustic soda (NaOH) is commonly used in advanced treatment to:
a. Increase pH and alkalinity
b. Decrease hardness
c. Remove TOC
d. Form chloramines
Back: Answer: a. Increase pH and alkalinity

Front:
Carbon dioxide addition to RO permeate is sometimes used to:
a. Increase alkalinity before lime or caustic addition
b. Disinfect water
c. Remove hardness
d. Remove color
Back: Answer: a. Increase alkalinity before lime or caustic addition

Front:
Sodium hypochlorite solutions gradually:
temperature
a. Decompose, losing strength over time, especially at high
b. Gain strength with time
c. Become less corrosive but more concentrated
d. Turn into caustic soda only
Back: Answer: a. Decompose, losing strength over time, especially at high

Front:
The best location to sample for UVT in a UV-AOP system is:
a. Immediately upstream of the UV reactor
b. In the raw water source
c. In the concentrate line
d. In the chemical storage room
Back: Answer: a. Immediately upstream of the UV reactor

Front:
UV lamps require less power to maintain dose than last month. Why?
a. Sleeve fouling
b. UVT increase
c. Lamp aging
d. Peroxide underfeed
Back: Answer: b. UVT increase

Front:
UV intensity sensors suddenly read higher than expected. Cause?
a. Sensor calibration drift
b. Sleeve fouling
c. Lamp failures
d. Analyzer wiring error
Back: Answer: a. Sensor calibration drift

Front:
UV-AOP reactor shows reduced peroxide consumption. Which is likely?
a. High UVT
b. High pH
c. Peroxide injection underfeed
d. Lamp overdrive
Back: Answer: c. Peroxide injection underfeed

Front:
UV sleeve fouling will cause:
a. Higher UVT
b. Lower UV intensity readings
c. Lower ORP
d. Higher dose for same power
Back: Answer: b. Lower UV intensity readings

Front:
UV lamps require higher power to maintain dose, but UVT is
unchanged. Cause?
a. Quartz sleeve fouling
b. High peroxide
c. Air entrainment
d. Analyzer drift
Back: Answer: a. Quartz sleeve fouling

Front:
UVT shows sudden drop from 92% to 86% with no upstream changes. Most
likely:
a. Analyzer fouling or stray light error
b. Lamp failure
c. Sleeve break
d. High pH
Back: Answer: a. Analyzer fouling or stray light error

Front:
UV radical generation decreases unexpectedly. Why?
a. High UVT
b. Lamp age
c. Peroxide under-dosing
d. High temperature
Back: Answer: c. Peroxide under-dosing

Front:
UV dose increases with:
a. Decreased UVT
b. Decreased flow rate (longer residence time)
c. Lamp fouling
d. Peroxide overfeed
Back: Answer: b. Decreased flow rate (longer residence time)

Front:
UV intensity decreases gradually while UVT is stable. Most likely
cause:
a. Quartz sleeve fouling
b. Lamp failure
c. High peroxide
d. High pH
Back: Answer: a. Quartz sleeve fouling

Front:
UV reactor shows increased headloss. Why?
a. Peroxide overdose
b. Quartz sleeve fouling or debris accumulation
c. Low UVT
d. High UV dose
Back: Answer: b. Quartz sleeve fouling or debris accumulation

Front:
UV-AOP uses peroxide as a radical promoter. A sudden drop in radical
production is likely due to:
a. High pH
b. Peroxide underfeed
c. UV overdrive
d. High ORP
Back: Answer: b. Peroxide underfeed

Front:
UV dose increases with:
a. Lower UVT
b. Longer hydraulic residence time
c. Lamp fouling
d. Lamp aging
Back: Answer: b. Longer hydraulic residence time

Front:
UVT decreases from 94% to 88%. The controller increases lamp power
to maintain dose. What is the primary operational concern?
a. Increased power consumption per unit of water treated
b. Excess production of hydroxyl radicals
c. Loss of NDMA destruction credit
d. Reduced RO recovery
Back: Answer: a. Increased power consumption per unit of water treated

Front:
Downstream peroxide residual is consistently higher than expected
after UV-AOP. What is the most likely explanation?
a. Excess peroxide is being overfed and is not fully consumed
b. UV dose is too low
c. UV dose is too high
d. Peroxide dose is too low
Back: Answer: a. Excess peroxide is being overfed and is not fully consumed

Front:
Reduced hydraulic mixing in a UV reactor poses which primary risk?
a. Higher UVT
b. Short-circuiting leading to under-dosed regions
c. Increased lamp fouling
d. Higher peroxide residual
Back: Answer: b. Short-circuiting leading to under-dosed regions

Front:
Which operating condition most increases bromate formation risk in
UV-AOP for high-bromide water?
a. High pH + high peroxide dose + high UV dose
b. Low pH + low UV dose
c. High pH + low UV dose
d. Low pH + high UV dose
Back: Answer: a. High pH + high peroxide dose + high UV dose

Front:
UV intensity sensors read low, but UVT and lamp age are normal. Most
likely issue?
a. Fouled or dirty UV sensor window
b. Lamp failure
c. Peroxide overdose
d. Valve misalignment
Back: Answer: a. Fouled or dirty UV sensor window

Front:
Peroxide consumption suddenly decreases in UV-AOP. Cause?
a. Lower UV dose
b. Peroxide underfeed or injection pump failure
c. High pH
d. High temperature
Back: Answer: b. Peroxide underfeed or injection pump failure

Front:
UV reactor pressure drop increases. Most likely cause:
a. Quartz sleeve fouling
b. High UVT
c. Low peroxide
d. Lamp overdrive
Back: Answer: a. Quartz sleeve fouling

Front:
UV dose reaches setpoint at lower lamp power than usual. Why?
a. UVT decreased
b. UVT increased
c. Peroxide residual high
d. Lamp fouling
Back: Answer: b. UVT increased

Front:
The primary purpose of UV AOP in advanced water treatment is to:
contaminants
a. Generate hydroxyl radicals for destruction of trace organic
b. Pasteurize water through heat transfer
c. Remove dissolved inorganic salts
d. Increase pH for downstream RO operation
Back: Answer: a. Generate hydroxyl radicals for destruction of trace organic

Front:
UV transmittance (UVT) is a critical parameter because it:
disinfection and oxidation performance
a. Determines how much UV light penetrates the water to achieve
b. Measures turbidity directly
c. Adjusts hydrogen peroxide dose automatically
d. Indicates lamp temperature
Back: Answer: a. Determines how much UV light penetrates the water to achieve

Front:
Which factor most reduces UV lamp output over time?
a. Lamp aging and gradual decline of arc efficiency
b. High UVT
c. Low water temperature
d. Reduced lamp power input
Back: Answer: a. Lamp aging and gradual decline of arc efficiency

Front:
In UV systems, fouling of quartz sleeves primarily causes:
a. Reduced UV intensity delivered to the water
b. Increased UV dose
c. Higher lamp temperature
d. Improved efficiency of RED
Back: Answer: a. Reduced UV intensity delivered to the water

Front:
In UV AOP, overdosing hydrogen peroxide has what operational effect?
a. Hydroxyl radical scavenging, which reduces oxidation efficiency
b. Increased UVT
c. Reduced consumption of peroxide
d. Improved RED consistency
Back: Answer: a. Hydroxyl radical scavenging, which reduces oxidation efficiency

Front:
The "Reduction Equivalent Dose" (RED) represents:
inactivation of microorganisms
a. The validated UV dose required to achieve a specific log
b. The maximum lamp output available
c. The dose delivered at the reactor inlet only
d. The ideal theoretical UV dose without losses
Back: Answer: a. The validated UV dose required to achieve a specific log

Front:
In UV reactors, the purpose of sleeve wiping systems is to: *a.
Remove fouling and maintain UV intensity
b. Reduce lamp power
c. Maintain water temperature
d. Increase RED beyond validated levels
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
Low UVT water entering a UV reactor will most likely require:
a. Higher lamp power or reduced flow to maintain dose
b. Lower RED setpoint
c. Higher pH adjustment
d. No operational change
Back: Answer: a. Higher lamp power or reduced flow to maintain dose

Front:
The generation of nitrite during UV exposure occurs primarily when:
a. Nitrate is present in the influent water
b. Free chlorine is high
c. H₂O₂ is overdosed
d. TDS is high
Back: Answer: a. Nitrate is present in the influent water

Front:
UV lamp efficiency is most sensitive to:
a. On/off cycling frequency
b. Turbidity below 0.1 NTU
c. pH changes
d. High dissolved oxygen
Back: Answer: a. On/off cycling frequency

Front:
In UV AOP, hydroxyl radicals are effective because:
contaminants
a. They are highly reactive and non-selective toward most organic
b. They persist for long periods in water
c. They improve disinfection only
d. They reduce scaling potential
Back: Answer: a. They are highly reactive and non-selective toward most organic

Front:
The parameter most affected when water temperature significantly
decreases in a UV system is:
a. Lamp output (lower at cold temperatures)
b. Peroxide decomposition rate increases
c. Quartz sleeve fouling rate increases
d. UVT improves automatically
Back: Answer: a. Lamp output (lower at cold temperatures)

Front:
The most common cause of UV intensity sensor drift is:
a. Sensor fouling or lack of calibration
b. High flow rate
c. Elevated nitrate levels
d. Reduced lamp age
Back: Answer: a. Sensor fouling or lack of calibration

Front:
In UV AOP, peroxide residual is monitored because:
treatment efficiency

c. It indicates permeate salinity

A drop in UVT following upstream RO treatment likely indicates:
a. Organic breakthrough or upstream contamination
b. Lamp failure in the UV reactor
c. Hydrogen peroxide overdosing
d. Increased feed temperature
Back: Answer: a. Organic breakthrough or upstream contamination

Front:
UV reactor validation is required to:
UVT conditions

Front:
In UV AOP, hydroxyl radicals are primarily formed when UV light
interacts with:
a. Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)
b. Chloramines
c. Ozone only
d. Calcium bicarbonate
Back: Answer: a. Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)

Front:
A decrease in UV intensity with stable UVT is most likely caused by:
a. Lamp aging or fouling of quartz sleeves
b. Increased NOM concentration
c. Higher nitrate levels
d. Reduced H₂O₂ feed
Back: Answer: a. Lamp aging or fouling of quartz sleeves

Front:
In UV disinfection, the delivered UV dose is directly proportional
to:
a. Intensity × exposure time
b. Water temperature only
c. Chlorine concentration
d. Feed TDS
Back: Answer: a. Intensity × exposure time

Front:
In UV AOP, which parameter must be closely controlled to maintain
consistent hydroxyl radical formation?
a. Hydrogen peroxide dose
b. Alkalinity
c. Silica concentration
d. Hardness
Back: Answer: a. Hydrogen peroxide dose

The primary objective of using the UV/H₂O₂ Advanced Oxidation
Process (AOP) is to:
conventional filtration.
alone.
refractory organic CECs.
scaling.

Front:
Which oxidation process is most effective for the destruction of
1,4-dioxane in an advanced water treatment system?
a. Chlorination followed by sedimentation.
b. Ozone only, without hydrogen peroxide.
c. UV/H₂O₂ Advanced Oxidation Process.
d. Slow sand filtration.
Back: Answer: c. UV/H₂O₂ Advanced Oxidation Process.

of a surrogate microorganism.

Front:

transmittance (UVT) after RO treatment. What is the primary reason
for this improvement?
UV light.

Front:
In UV AOP systems, which water quality parameter most significantly
reduces hydroxyl radical efficiency?
a. Low temperature.
b. High dissolved oxygen concentration.
c. High nitrate, bicarbonate, or carbonate concentrations.
d. Low alkalinity.
Back: Answer: c. High nitrate, bicarbonate, or carbonate concentrations.

Front:
When hydrogen peroxide is overdosed in UV AOP systems:
a. Hydroxyl radical generation increases exponentially.
b. UV dose increases proportionally.
c. Hydroxyl radicals are scavenged, reducing AOP efficiency.
d. No significant impact occurs.
Back: Answer: c. Hydroxyl radicals are scavenged, reducing AOP efficiency.

Front:
A utility operating a UV AOP system observes that UVT drops suddenly
from 98% to 85%. What is the most likely cause?
a. Lamp aging beyond 12,000 hours.
b. Increased hydrogen peroxide dosing.
c. An increase in dissolved organic matter entering the UV reactor.
d. A decrease in reactor flow rate.
Back: Answer: c. An increase in dissolved organic matter entering the UV reactor.

Front:
In a UV reactor, sleeve fouling most significantly impacts which
parameter?
a. Flow rate through the reactor.
b. Lamp electrical efficiency.
c. UV intensity delivered to the water.
d. Temperature of the reactor chamber.
Back: Answer: c. UV intensity delivered to the water.

Front:
In UV AOP, the main purpose of adding hydrogen peroxide is to:
a. Increase UV lamp efficiency.
b. Reduce nitrate formation.
c. Generate hydroxyl radicals when exposed to UV light.
d. Neutralize carbonate ions.
Back: Answer: c. Generate hydroxyl radicals when exposed to UV light.

Front:
Which AOP byproduct may form when nitrate is exposed to UV light?
a. Bromate.
b. Free chlorine.
c. Nitrite.
d. Chlorite.
Back: Answer: c. Nitrite.

Front:
In UV systems, what is the effect of overcooling lamp sleeves?
a. Increased UV intensity.
b. Decreased lamp efficiency.
c. Higher RED value.
d. Increased hydroxyl radical production.
Back: Answer: b. Decreased lamp efficiency.

Front:
In UV AOP, hydroxyl radicals are effective primarily because they:
contaminants.
a. Selectively oxidize aromatic compounds only.
b. React only with inorganic species.
c. Are highly reactive and non-selective toward most organic
d. Can be stored in solution for long periods.
Back: Answer: c. Are highly reactive and non-selective toward most organic

Front:
In UV systems, lamp output is most directly proportional to:
a. Water temperature.
b. pH.
c. Hydrogen peroxide concentration.
d. Lamp current (power input).
Back: Answer: d. Lamp current (power input).
